newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S., Mexico renew energy cooperation.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Mexico renew energy cooperation.

text.p: U.S. Energy Secretary Federico Pena and Jesus Reyes Heroles agreed to tighten energy cooperation, reviving a stagnant 14-year-old technology project, a senior U.S. energy official said on Tuesday.
The two cabinet members talked in Spanish for two and a half hours as part of the annual Binational Commission meetings held here on Monday.
"They decided to reenergize the energy technology bilateral working group established in 1983," the official, who declined to be named, said in a phone interview.

The group will focus on air quality work, rural electrification and perpetual forestry, among other topics, he said. Meetings will be at least once a year, beginning probably in October in the United States.

The group will study improving Mexico's air quality, specifically in highly polluted Mexico City. Through promoting cleaner gasolines and natural gas instead of fuel oil and liquified petroleum gas (LPG), Mexico has been working to reduce pollution.
"Secretary Pena pointed out the air patterns in Mexico City are very similar to those in Denver, where he was mayor," the official said.

Other possible future projects include trade of excess U.S. power south of the border, the official said, adding that the restructuring of U.S. power plants could result in a marketable quantity of power.
"A lot of excess power could be routed to the Mexican side of the border, where demand for power is growing much more rapidly," he said.
The U.S. Department of Energy said in a statement that integration of North American energy markets should reduce costs and improve efficiencies.
"But more needs to be done in adopting compatible structures and removing trade and investment barriers to more fully integrate our energy markets," the statement said.
The two cabinet members also discussed investment opportunities for U.S. companies amid an expected boom in Mexico's energy demand. While investment prospects in natural
gas distribution look encouraging, the petrochemical industry privatization has been less enticing, the official said.
Mexico changed its scheme for selling off the sector, reducing private ownership to 49 percent in existing plants while allowing full ownership over any new plants.

"U.S. companies are not pleased with the 49 percent ownership (in existing petrochemical plants)," he said. "I think there is concern over where the feedstock will be coming from and what it will be like for the new facility to compete with Pemex (Petroleos Mexicanos) facilities."

He hailed progress in privatizing natural gas distribution and the regulatory framework for selling off rights to the fuel, which will continue to be supplied by state oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex).
